ulation of platelet aggregation
Platelets are corpuscles without nuclei derived from the fragmentation of megakaryocytes, which play a fundamental role in hemo-
stasis. Platelet activity is triggered by primary stimuli (collagen, thrombin, adrenaline) and by substances that can be released by
activated platelets themselves (serotonin, ADP, calcium ions, platelet activating factor (PAF) and TXA2). There are also inhibitory
factors, such as prostacyclin (PGI2) and nitric oxide (NO). All these substances appear to have speciﬁc receptors on the platelet
membrane (Imig, 2020). Fig. 6 summarizes the mechanisms of the platelet response following stimulation of some of these
receptors.

The interaction between primary stimuli and platelet substances with receptors results in the release of calcium ions from the
dense tubular system into the cytoplasmic space. In this cellular compartment, calcium ions stimulate calmodulin, leading to phos-
phorylation of the myosin light chains, which ﬁnally causes the actomyosinic contraction responsible for platelet shape changes and
platelet movements.
The release of calcium ions into the cytosol can be considered the fundamental mechanism for triggering platelet activity. The
